title: Crazy You < Sane You
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart borrows Brené Brown's observation that self-aware acknowledgment of one's own irrationality is what constitutes sanity, and applies this framing to teacher stress. The article's central argument is that over-pressure degrades teaching quality — a stressed teacher is a less effective teacher — and that this is a professional concern as much as a personal one. Stuart invokes the Yerkes-Dodson curve to explain why excessive pressure places teachers on the wrong side of the performance-arousal relationship, producing both worse instructional outcomes and lower life enjoyment simultaneously. He argues that escaping this state requires not only strategic adjustments (simplifying, satisficing) but deeper inner work about the meaning and acceptable limits of one's labor. The closing frames the goal of teaching as being a good teacher — not the best or a perfect one — and presents this as a journey that demands sustainable sanity rather than heroic overextension.
points: An over-pressured teacher is a less effective teacher — teacher stress is not only a personal problem but a professional one with direct instructional consequences.
The Yerkes-Dodson curve explains the double penalty: when pressure exceeds the optimal zone, both performance and life enjoyment decline simultaneously.
Relief from over-stress requires inner work as well as strategy shifts — revisiting why one teaches and making peace with labor whose fruits may never be fully visible.
Satisficing and asking 'what would this look like if it were simple?' are tactical tools, but they only help when paired with settled answers to deeper questions about purpose and limits.
Brené Brown's framing — that grappling with one's irrationality is what makes a person sane — grounds the article's core insight that self-aware teachers are better teachers.
quotes: Brene Brown has this line that I love, and I heard it in a talk so what follows is perhaps a paraphrase: "There are two kinds of people in the world: crazy people who know they are crazy and crazy people who do not." To Brown, what makes a person sane is grappling with their insanity; it's the ignoring of insanity, the pretending it's not there, that makes our mental imbalances unlivable.
When you and me get all stressed out and crazy about this teaching job of ours, we're less of a teacher than when we're calm and sane.
This isn't just a personal problem; it's a professional one. When we get into this place of WAY TOO MUCH PRESSURE, we end up on the wrong side of the Yerkes-Dodson curve.
When I'm over-pressured and overworked — when my yoke is heavy and burdensome — I get hit by the rough and rude double whammy. 1. My performance declines. 2. My life enjoyment declines, too.

Whenever I find myself going nuts about teaching, the solutions are rarely easy. They often require not just changes in my strategy but lots of inner work, too (e.g., What is my class all about? Why am I a teacher? What is the good I am seeking to do through my labor — and if I never fully see the fruit of that work, can I be okay with that?)

My goal in teaching isn't to be the best teacher and definitely not to be a perfect one. It's to be a good teacher. This is an ongoing journey that teaching reliably calls me into, and my life and soul are better for having done this kind of work for twenty years.
